subject: Accounting
title: Who Are the Big Four?
description: One-minute skill: Who Are the Big Four?.

hook.text: Four firms audit most of the world's largest companies: Deloitte, PwC, EY, and KPMG.

buildup.text: Together they employ over a million people and generate more than $200 billion in annual revenue.

discovery.text: They audit over 80% of all U.S. public companies and nearly every Fortune 500 firm.

twist.text: Before Enron, there were five. Arthur Andersen's collapse created an oligopoly that still exists.

climax.text: Critics worry that too few firms auditing too many companies creates systemic risk.

punchline.text: Four firms guard the world's financial truth. Is that enough?

quiz.question: Why are there only four major audit firms today?
options: Arthur Andersen collapsed after the Enron scandal

details.summary: The Big Four — Deloitte, PwC, EY, and KPMG — are the four largest accounting and professional services firms in the world, auditing the vast majority of large public companies and generating over $200 billion in combined annual revenue.
details.whyItMatters: The Big Four's dominance of the audit market raises important questions about competition, conflicts of interest, and systemic risk when so few firms are responsible for auditing the world's largest companies.
takeaways: The Big Four are Deloitte, PricewaterhouseCoopers, Ernst & Young, and KPMG
They audit more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies and most large public companies globally
Their dominance creates concentration risk — losing one firm would cause a systemic crisis

faq.question: Why are there only four dominant accounting firms?
faq.answer: There used to be eight major firms, then six, then five. Mergers consolidated the industry, and Arthur Andersen's collapse after Enron eliminated one more. The barriers to entry — global networks, regulatory expertise, reputation — make it extremely difficult for smaller firms to compete.

faq.question: Is the Big Four's dominance a problem?
faq.answer: Many regulators and academics think so. If one of the four collapsed, there wouldn't be enough capacity to audit all large public companies. Their consulting businesses also create potential conflicts of interest. Several countries have considered mandatory rotation or structural reforms.
